extracted.intended_audience: historians and scholars of technology, culture, and futurology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for analyzing writings and rhetoric about the future (futurist literature, technological forecasts, national/imperial projections), focusing on themes, political functions, and assumptions. Useful for scholars assessing the form, function, and historical accuracy of future-oriented texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-as-exhortation
rubrics_metrics.description: The future is used as a rhetorical exhortation to revitalize optimism, call for public faith, and embellish or mask present political and social problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the text invokes a ‘sublime technological future’ to elevate commonplaces (world fairs, centennial expositions, official orations). Examples: Centennial Exhibition (1876) rhetoric, Roosevelt’s inaugurals, civic commissions on national goals. Anti-pattern: rhetoric that discounts present injustices (labor unrest, racial inequality, economic depression) by promising Tomorrow as solvent. Scoring note: higher concern when exhortation functions to ward off dissent or provide ‘pseudo-unity’.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-as-ideological_fulfillment (literary prophecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The future is presented as the fulfillment of a specific ideology or idealism, rewriting the past and present to show a coming epoch that vindicates those beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the narrative reconstrues history/present to make technological or policy promises appear inevitable (e.g., claims that particular technologies will yield 'peace, democracy, and ecological harmony'). Example: imperial futurist literature projecting Pax Britannica or American destiny. Anti-pattern: conflating technological adoption with deterministic ideological victory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future-as_technological_exorcism/participatory_forecasting
rubrics_metrics.description: The future is framed as produced by information-processing technologies and public participation in data extrapolation, presented as a method to cleanse confusion and correct human fallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for appeals to collecting data, trend extrapolation, and 'participatory' forecasting (opinion polling, information utilities) as proof of reliable future-making. Example: notions of electronic consultation reviving democracy (Birkenhead) or National Goals Research Staff. Warning: such participation may be ceremonial; evaluate whether it transfers real power or merely simulates consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological_determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: An assumption that new communications and transportation technologies will be the primary drivers that resolve social problems and radically reorder society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for claims that electricity, railways, telegraph, radio, computers, or automation will ‘eliminate’ social ills (drudgery, class conflict, isolation). Examples: Garvey, Mumford, Toffler, Reich. Anti-pattern: ignoring economic/political structures that shape technological deployment; historical counterexamples include persistence of inequality despite electrification or TVA's environmental harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utopian_environmental/social_outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The future is depicted as a landscape of environmental balance, social harmony, and peace resulting from technological progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify promises of a radiant landscape, integration of town and country, ecological balance, or end of warfare. Examples: Mumford’s ‘intermarriage of town and country,’ Geddes’s ‘Eutopia.’ Scoring: question feasibility and whether the text addresses trade-offs or unintended consequences (e.g., hydroelectric projects that uprooted environments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escapism_or_deflection_from_present_problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Futurist rhetoric functions as a form of consolation or ‘false consciousness,’ diverting attention from present structural conflicts (wealth/status struggles, racial injustice, labor issues) toward an imagined future where these problems disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the text asks readers to 'retain faith in the future' as a remedy for present grievances (C. Wright Mills, Huxley critique). Example: rhetoric that urges belief in shared future to maintain national unity while ignoring substantive present conflicts. Anti-pattern: treating future promise as substitute for political reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recycling_of_past_futures (today’s future is yesterday’s future)
rubrics_metrics.description: Futurist narratives reuse earlier tropes and symbols (machines, exhibitions, empire) rather than offering genuinely novel predictions, making 'today's future' substantially similar to past visions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect continuity with nineteenth-century symbols (Corliss engine, Great Exhibition) in modern projections (satellites, computers). Example: parallels between 1876 Centennial imagery and late twentieth-century space/computer imagery. Implication: evaluate originality and sensitivity to historical recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial_rebranding_after_failure
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior future predictions fail, authors or institutions offer a new future narrative to patch up prior miscarriages of prophecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify patterns where failed promises are met by invoking another 'new future' rather than reassessing underlying premises. Example: successive centennial/bi-centennial commissions; successive technological panaceas. Scoring: negative when reassignment of faith substitutes for accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite_or_imperial_bias_in_futurism
rubrics_metrics.description: Futurist visions often serve elite or imperial interests, valorizing empire, national prestige, or ruling-class amenities under the guise of universal progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for projections that normalize or justify imperial structures, patrols, and elite comforts (Birkenhead’s RAF/pipelines, Pax Britannica fantasies). Example: imperial futurist literature used to rationalize expenditure and suppress revolutionary ideologies. Assess whose interests the projected future serves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technocracy_and_simulated_democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Futurist schemes propose governance by experts or specialist cadres, often accompanied by electronic consultation that masks a continued concentration of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims that broadcasting, opinion polling, or electronic consultation will revive ancient forms of direct democracy but in practice centralize authority in experts (Birkenhead, Toffler). Anti-pattern: ‘consultation’ that is a mere formality; presence of specialists attached to social groups to solicit consent rather than devolve authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect_of_political_and_economic_factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Futurist visions that focus on technological change often neglect political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape outcomes, leading to mistaken predictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the account addresses political economy (labor organization, managerialism, military-industrial alignments) or simply attributes change to technology. Examples: Mumford’s recognition of 'miscarriage of the machine'; TVA becoming technocratic and environmentally damaging. Scoring: stronger analyses explicitly engage political/economic constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralization_and_regionalist_alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative futurist criterion emphasizing dispersion of production, regional cultures, and ecological rehabilitation (Kropotkin, Geddes, Mumford’s neotechnic visions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposals for 'industrial villages,' electricity enabling decentralization, and 'partnership of man and nature.' Example: Geddes’s and Kropotkin’s visions and their influence on American conservationists. Evaluate realism and attention to political feasibility; Mumford cautions about neglect of political facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical_accuracy_and_unintended_consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether forecasts anticipated negative unintended consequences or misread the social effects of technologies (e.g., environmental damage, continued centralization, persistence of class conflict).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical case studies (TVA, hydroelectric projects, automation promises) to judge whether the forecaster considered nontechnical impacts. Anti-pattern: triumphalist predictions that ignore long-term environmental, social, or political harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication-centric_periodization
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess claims that major social transformations are primarily communication revolutions (printing, electrified mass media, information utilities) and whether the forecaster justifies the scale and mechanism of such shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the argument that the era is defined by communication and control (Wiener), and whether the analysis carefully links technological capability (signal reproduction, broadband info utilities) to plausible societal rearrangements. Example: distinguishing printing, electricity/telegraph era, and current computer/utility phase; examine evidentiary basis and limits of extrapolation.
